unitTargets: •  I can explain how fossils and radiometric dating tell geologists about Earth's past.
•  I can describe the geologic time scale and place the Precambrian eons within it.
•  I can describe what life, the surface, and the climate looked like in each geologic period, Cambrian through Quaternary.
•  I can trace how supercontinents assembled and broke apart across Earth's history.
•  I can describe the cause and scale of Earth's major mass extinction events.

•  Siberian Traps, Chicxulub, iridium layer, K–Pg boundary

sectionsContent.title: The Geologic Time Scale
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe how geologists build the geologic time scale and read Earth's history from fossils and rock layers.

notes.key: Bones, teeth, shells, wood, and leaves — preserved parts of an organism. Durable tissues are more likely to survive.
Tracks, trails, burrows, and coprolites — records of biological activity. The organism itself may be absent.
Minerals fill pores in buried wood, bone, or shell; original material may remain.
Minerals substitute for original material as it dissolves; petrified wood can show both processes.
Burial flattens remains; a thin carbon film may preserve a leaf or fern.
A mold is a hollow impression left after buried material dissolves or decays; a cast is sediment or minerals filling that mold, making a 3-D replica.

notes: *Most fossils occur in sedimentary rock, where layers of sediment bury and preserve remains.

cues: Best method for very old rock vs. recent organic material

notes.key: Measuring a radioactive parent isotope and its decay products to find a mineral's age.
The time it takes for half of the parent atoms in a sample to decay.

notes.text: Best method for very old rock, and for recent organic material:
notes.key: Uranium-lead and potassium-argon date very ancient rock. Carbon-14 dates material younger than about 50,000 years.

notes: *A mineral's age usually records when it crystallized — not necessarily the age of the whole rock layer around it.

About 4.54 billion years ago.

sectionsContent.title: Eons, Eras, Epochs & Periods
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe the Precambrian's place in Earth's history and the major events of its three eons.

cues: Share of Earth's history it covers

notes.text: Share of Earth's history it covers:
notes.key: An informal span (not a true eon) covering about 88% of Earth's history.

notes.text: The three eons, oldest to youngest:
notes.key: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic.
Earth accretes and differentiates; dense iron-rich metal sinks to form the core.
Long-lived crust, oceans, and microbial ecosystems develop.
Atmospheric oxygen rises; eukaryotes and later multicellular organisms diversify.

cues: Great Oxidation Event — timing and cause
Snowball Earth — timing and the two episodes
rows.notesLabel: OXYGEN AND ICE IN THE PROTEROZOIC

notes.text: Great Oxidation Event — timing and cause:
notes.key: Began about 2.4 billion years ago, as photosynthesis released oxygen faster than rocks and iron could absorb it.

notes.text: Snowball Earth — timing and the two episodes:
notes.key: The Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations, roughly 720–635 million years ago.

notes: *Rising oxygen was toxic to many anaerobic microbes but made complex, oxygen-using life possible.

sectionsContent.summaryPrompt: In your own words: what changed on Earth, in order, across the Hadean, Archean, and Proterozoic?
selfCheck: I can name the three Precambrian eons in order.
I can explain why the Great Oxidation Event was a turning point.

sectionsContent.title: Period-by-Period Deep Dive
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe what life, the surface, and the climate looked like in each geologic period.

notes.key: Shallow seas spread across continental margins; sand, mud, and carbonate sediments become sandstone, shale, and limestone. Laurentia includes the core of modern North America.

The Cambrian Explosion (about 539 million years ago) rapidly diversifies animal body plans — arthropods (trilobites), mollusks, brachiopods, sponges, echinoderms, and early chordates appear. Life is still entirely marine.
Greenhouse conditions and high sea levels are widespread; atmospheric oxygen is lower than today.

notes: *The Cambrian Explosion happened over tens of millions of years, not overnight — and rare sites like the Burgess Shale preserve soft-bodied animals that ordinary fossilization loses.

notes.key: Shallow seas cover large areas; plate collisions begin new phases of mountain building.
Marine biodiversity expands — reefs and jawless fishes flourish — while major extinctions follow the late-period cooling, and early land plants appear.
Warm conditions give way to late-Ordovician cooling, ice growth, and falling sea level.
Laurentia and Baltica converge during Caledonian mountain building; much of Gondwana sits at southern latitudes.
Jawed fishes and eurypterids diversify; small vascular plants and terrestrial arthropods expand the first land communities and soils.
Warming after the Ordovician glaciation helps sea levels recover.
Continental collisions continue; reefs thrive in warm shallow seas.
Placoderms, early cartilaginous fish, and lobe-finned fish diversify in the sea; forests, insects, and early tetrapods spread on land — before late-Devonian extinctions hit hard.
Warm shallow-sea conditions persist before late-Devonian environmental crises disrupt them.
Pangaea assembles through major continental collisions; Appalachian mountain building continues; tropical wetlands bury thick organic deposits that later become coal.

Giant arthropods (Meganeura, Arthropleura) and diversifying amphibians dominate wet habitats on land; the amniotic egg lets early reptiles and synapsids reproduce away from water; sharks and reef organisms fill shallow seas.
Tropical regions stay warm and humid while southern Gondwana glaciates; oxygen rises above modern levels as CO₂ declines.

notes: *The amniotic egg let vertebrates reproduce away from standing water for the first time — a major step toward life fully on land.

notes.key: Pangaea is fully assembled, surrounded by one ocean (Panthalassa); interior regions far from the coast are strongly seasonal and dry.
Synapsids (the mammal lineage, e.g. Dimetrodon) and sauropsids (the reptile and dinosaur-ancestor lineage) diverge; amphibians, insects, sharks, and marine invertebrates remain important.
Conditions vary through the period; by the end of the Permian, severe warming and widespread ocean oxygen loss set up a crisis.

notes: *Dimetrodon is a synapsid — the mammal lineage — not a dinosaur, even though it looked reptilian.

notes.key: Pangaea remains largely assembled through most of the period, but late-Triassic rifting begins the breakup that continues into the Jurassic.
Ecosystems rebuild after the end-Permian crisis; reptile groups diversify, and dinosaurs appear later in the period.
Interior regions are often hot, dry, and strongly seasonal.

notes: *Dinosaurs first appear in the Triassic — roughly 230 million years ago — but are not yet the dominant land animals.

notes.key: New ocean basins (the Atlantic, the Gulf of Mexico) open as Pangaea continues splitting apart.

Giant sauropods (Diplodocus, Brachiosaurus) and theropods (Allosaurus) dominate on land; ichthyosaurs and other marine reptiles fill ocean food webs; pterosaurs (flying reptiles, not dinosaurs) are common in the air. Archaeopteryx, a feathered dinosaur near the origin of birds, dates to about 150 million years ago.
Greenhouse conditions are widespread; shallow seas cover large areas, leaving extensive rock records in places like western Europe.

notes: *Ichthyosaurs and pterosaurs are reptiles, not dinosaurs — the 'Age of Dinosaurs' also had non-dinosaur reptiles ruling the sea and air.

notes.key: High sea levels flood broad continental areas; continued continental breakup reshapes coastlines and currents; even Antarctica supports forests during warm intervals.

Flowering plants (angiosperms) spread and diversify, with insects diversifying alongside them; diverse dinosaur groups (including ceratopsians) and early birds flourish; mammals are already present, though small, before the period ends in mass extinction.
Greenhouse conditions and high sea levels dominate most of the period.

notes: *Paleontologists learn about dinosaurs from fossils — skulls and bones for identity, tracks and eggs for behavior, and dated rock layers for when they lived and died out.

notes.key: Continents keep moving toward modern positions; converging plates begin building the Alpine–Himalayan belt (India colliding with Asia) and the Circum-Pacific belt (Andes, western North America, Japan).
Mammals diversify rapidly into the ecological space left open after the K–Pg extinction.
Climate cools gradually as the greenhouse conditions of the Mesozoic fade.
Continued plate motion and mountain building (Himalaya, Andes) keep reshaping the continents.
Grasslands spread widely as climates change, and grazing mammals diversify alongside them.
Global climate cools further and dries in many regions.
Continental ice sheets advance and retreat repeatedly, reaching several kilometers thick and reshaping drainage, soils, and landforms.
Modern mammal and bird lineages diversify further; primates and whales evolve within this era; human evolution occurs during the Quaternary's repeated glacial cycles.

Many glacial cycles alternate with warmer interglacials, paced by Milankovitch orbital cycles — eccentricity (~100,000 years), obliquity/tilt (~41,000 years), and precession (~19,000–23,000 years). The Holocene is the current interglacial.

notes: *The Pleistocene ran from 2.58 million years ago to 11,700 years ago; we now live in the Holocene, the current interglacial.

sectionsContent.title: Supercontinents Through Time
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can trace how supercontinents assembled and broke apart across Earth's history.

notes.key: Assembled roughly 1.1–0.9 billion years ago, during the Proterozoic.
Assembled during the Permian Period; began rifting apart in the Late Triassic Period.

notes.text: Reading a paleo-map — white outlines show:
notes.key: Where modern continental regions sit on the ancient map.

notes: *A single ocean, Panthalassa, surrounded Pangaea; the Tethys Sea sat along its eastern margin.

selfCheck: I can name both supercontinents in this unit and roughly when each existed.

sectionsContent.title: Mass Extinction Events
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe the cause and scale of Earth's two largest mass extinctions in this unit.

notes.key: About 252 million years ago, ending the Paleozoic Era.
Siberian Traps volcanism — huge eruptions and intrusions released greenhouse gases directly and by heating carbon-rich rocks, driving global warming and ocean oxygen loss.
Most marine species disappeared, and land ecosystems suffered severe losses; rebuilding complex ecosystems took millions of years.
About 66 million years ago, ending the Mesozoic Era.
A roughly 10 km asteroid struck near today's Yucatán Peninsula (the Chicxulub crater).
An iridium-enriched layer worldwide, shocked minerals, impact spherules, tsunami deposits, and the Chicxulub crater itself.
About 75% of species disappeared, including all non-avian dinosaurs.

notes: *Birds are theropod dinosaurs, and they survived the K–Pg extinction — the dinosaur lineage continues today.
